strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: calibration under distribution shift without access to target-domain information, which is genuinely useful for safety-critical deployment.

Extensive and broad empirical evaluation across synthetic (CIFAR-10/100-C, Tiny-ImageNet-C), real-world (Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), and semantic (Office-Home) shift benchmarks, plus CNN and transformer backbones (ViT, Swin, DeiT).

Thorough ablations that isolate the filtering and rectification components, compare against symmetric multi-objective gradient methods (PCGrad, CAGrad), and test compatibility with alternative calibration losses (Soft-AvUC, MMCE, Brier) and post-hoc temperature scaling.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: hyperparameters, training configurations, two-stage fine-tuning, batch-size/rho/lambda sensitivity, feature-space Wasserstein analysis, and wall-clock compute comparisons are all reported; a code release is promised.

The paper is largely honest about limitations (covariate-shift focus, DCT dependence, limited gains on semantic shift, added training cost), and the projection property is stated correctly as an optimizer-level, asymmetric constrained update rather than a scalarized joint loss.
weaknesses: Limited originality: both core ingredients are established. DCT low-pass filtering to suppress high-frequency shortcut cues is well known (Yin et al. 2019; Fridovich-Keil et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2023), and the rectification rule is essentially PCGrad's projection (Yu et al. 2020) applied one-sidedly. The 'asymmetric' variant is a minor modification, and Proposition 4.1 is a trivial half-space projection result giving only a first-order non-increase of the training calibration loss—a very weak guarantee that says nothing about test-time calibration.

A critical baseline is missing: Soft-ECE (or any pure calibration loss) used as a standalone training-time method is never compared directly. Since FGR's calibration gradient is exactly Soft-ECE, the absence of this baseline makes it impossible to judge how much of the gain comes from gradient rectification versus simply adding a Soft-ECE regularizer. 'Rect. Only' and 'Weighted Sum' are not clean substitutes.

Some reported numbers are internally suspicious or inconsistent and are not explained: e.g., CIFAR-10-C CE has ECE 23.51 but CECE 4.87 and ACE 4.38, and Tiny-ImageNet-C CE has ECE 25.83 yet 'w/ TS' 36.23 (TS increases ECE). Metric scales differ by orders of magnitude across datasets (CECE ~3-5 on CIFAR-C vs ~10-19 on Camelyon17 vs ~0.15-0.4 on iWildCam), which raises concerns about consistent metric computation. No standard deviations/error bars are reported despite three runs.

The claimed 'significant' improvements are not uniform: on FMoW FGR (25.06) is only marginally better than Mixup (25.16), and on iWildCam it is roughly on par with several baselines. The headline reductions are concentrated on Camelyon17 and synthetic corruptions.

Mechanistic justification is weak: it is unclear why filtering only 5% of images (rho=0.05) should materially change learned features toward domain invariance, and the evidence for the 'domain-invariant features' claim is mostly correlational (Grad-CAM and reliability diagrams). The Wasserstein analysis measures D_orig vs D_mix feature distance, not cross-domain invariance, so it does not substantiate the central mechanism.

In several places FGR trades accuracy for calibration (e.g., iWildCam test Acc 75.22 vs PCGrad 77.21; Camelyon17 87.37 vs PCGrad 88.68), which complicates the claim of 'preserving ID performance.' BSCE-GRA is manually re-implemented, adding risk of unfair comparison.

Presentation/carelessness issues: reference years are inconsistent with in-text citations (e.g., Cao et al. 2021 vs 2024, Geirhos 2023 vs 2020, Dosovitskiy 2020 vs 2021, Chen 2024 vs 2026), and equation numbering jumps from (4) to (6), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

strengths: Targets a genuinely important and practical problem—target-agnostic calibration under distribution shift—and evaluates it broadly (synthetic corruptions, real-world WILDS datasets, semantic shift on Office-Home, and transformer backbones), which is more thorough than many calibration papers.

The two-component design (DCT low-pass filtering + gradient rectification) is intuitive and the ablation tables (Filter Only / Rect. Only / Weighted Sum / FGR) attempt to isolate the contributions of each component rather than reporting only the combined system.

The authors explicitly and honestly clarify the asymmetric, one-sided nature of the rectification and state that it is not equivalent to minimizing a fixed weighted sum of losses, avoiding overclaiming on that point; they also include a limitations section (Appendix F).
The first-order preservation framing is stated clearly, and the paper compares against PCGrad/CAGrad, which is the right family of baselines for the gradient-manipulation idea.
weaknesses: Limited originality. DCT-based low-pass filtering and gradient-projection conflict resolution (PCGrad) are both well-established; the contribution is essentially an asymmetric, one-sided variant of PCGrad bolted onto a known filtering trick. The claimed 'theoretical guarantee' (Proposition 4.1) is near-tautological—it asserts that the Euclidean projection of a vector onto a half-space lies in that half-space—and offers no accumulation, convergence, or generalization guarantee. The constraint is only on the per-batch Soft-ECE proxy on training data, not on held-out or shifted calibration.

Evidential concerns about the reported metrics. ECE and CECE differ by orders of magnitude (e.g., Tiny-ImageNet-C CE: ECE 25.83 vs CECE 0.44; CIFAR-10-C CE: ECE 23.51 vs CECE 4.87), and the 'w/ TS' columns sometimes increase ECE (Tiny-ImageNet-C CE: 25.83 → 36.23), which is anomalous for temperature scaling and suggests inconsistent or buggy metric computation. This undermines confidence in the headline numbers and in the central claim of large calibration gains.

No variance or error bars are reported despite the claim of averaging over three seeds, while many improvements over strong baselines are within noise (FMoW FGR ECE 25.06 vs Mixup 25.16; iWildCam FGR 3.34 vs Mixup 3.50). The significance of the improvements is therefore unclear.

Fairness of the comparison is questionable. FGR stacks DFL + Soft-ECE + filtering + rectification, whereas several baselines are far simpler (CE, LS). The most informative internal comparison (Weighted Sum) shows small margins over FGR in some cases (CIFAR-10-C: 7.93 vs 6.78; CIFAR-100-C: 11.80 vs 10.50) and anomalous behavior in others (iWildCam Weighted Sum Test ECE 11.17, worse than either of its components), so the specific benefit of the rectification mechanism—the paper's nominal main contribution—is not convincingly established. Ablations suggest filtering drives most of the shifted-calibration gain.

The central premise that 'distribution shifts predominantly alter high-frequency visual patterns' is asserted with thin support, and it is not clear that filtering only ρ = 5% of training samples could induce the claimed feature-level shift. The only direct evidence that the model relies more on domain-invariant (low-frequency) features is qualitative Grad-CAM, which is weak.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code URL ('Our code is available at' with no link) and by ad hoc per-dataset/architecture focusing parameters (Tables 9–10), with no clear evidence that baselines' hyperparameters (e.g., the weighted-sum weight) were tuned comparably.

The advantage of the proposed asymmetric rectification over symmetric multi-objective methods is modest and inconsistent; in some settings (Camelyon17, iWildCam) PCGrad attains higher shifted accuracy, and the paper leans on the ECE advantage without establishing robustness of that gap.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: maintaining calibrated confidence under distribution shift without target-domain access. The target-agnostic setting is well motivated and useful for real-world deployment.

The proposed FGR method combines DCT-based low-pass filtering with an asymmetric gradient-rectification scheme. The projection formulation is simple, weight-free, and supported by a correct proposition showing first-order non-increase of the ID calibration loss.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing in scope: synthetic corruptions (CIFAR-10/100-C, TinyImageNet-C), real-world WILDS shifts (Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW), semantic shift (Office-Home), and transformer backbones. The method consistently improves ECE/CECE/ACE while largely preserving or improving accuracy.

The paper includes useful ablations that isolate filtering and rectification, comparisons with PCGrad/CAGrad and a weighted-sum variant, gradient-conflict analysis, start-epoch and batch-size sensitivity, computational-cost analysis, and a two-stage fine-tuning variant.

Reproducibility is generally strong: the appendix provides pseudocode, dataset details, model configurations, hyperparameters, implementation notes for baselines, proofs, and a limitations section. The paper also includes an ethics/impact statement.
The theoretical analysis is modest but appropriate, and the paper is careful to describe the guarantee as first-order and batch-local rather than overclaiming an exact global constraint.
weaknesses: The central premise that distribution shifts predominantly alter high-frequency patterns is plausible and well cited, but it is not directly validated in this work. A control experiment with a generic low-pass filter (e.g., Gaussian blur or JPEG compression at matched strength) would better isolate whether the benefit is specifically frequency-aware or simply due to stronger augmentation/regularization.

Empirical gains are consistent but often moderate rather than dramatic. For example, on TinyImageNet-C FGR achieves ECE 12.39 versus 13.08 for BSCE-GRA, and on FMoW 25.06 versus 26.59 for DFL. The claim of 'significant' improvement is somewhat overstated for several settings.

Hyperparameter sensitivity remains a practical concern. The focusing parameter gamma is tuned per dataset and architecture with values ranging roughly from 1.2 to 5.5, the FGR start epoch is fixed at 200 after sensitivity analysis, and rho/lambda are also dataset-dependent. This shifts rather than eliminates the tuning burden and may limit ease of deployment on new datasets.

The theoretical guarantee only ensures first-order non-increase of the ID calibration loss on the sampled batch. It does not directly guarantee improved calibration under distribution shift, which remains an empirical claim driven mainly by the filtering component.

Some metric reporting is unclear or potentially inconsistent. In Table 1, for TinyImageNet-C, CE has ECE 25.83 but CECE 0.44 and ACE 0.43; the units and scale for CECE/ACE are not clearly stated, making it difficult to interpret the magnitude of these results.

The comparison against a weighted-sum baseline is close in several settings, but the paper does not show sensitivity to the weighted-sum coefficient. The claimed advantage of avoiding a loss-balancing coefficient is therefore only partially substantiated.
Some baselines, notably BSCE-GRA, were manually implemented, and the code link is missing in the manuscript. These are minor but worth noting for reproducibility.
The method is limited to image classification under covariate shift and shows weaker gains on semantic shift; the authors acknowledge this, but it reduces the generality of the contribution.
